sense: give out, run short; let someone down

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation (-iō); intransitive, or with an accusative of the person failed
evidence: Caes. BG 7.50 (Lewis & Short): quem jam sanguis vīrēsque dēficiunt
Hor. Epist. 1.11.30: animus sī tē nōn dēficit aequus
terms.comment: Of strength, voice, light, money, supplies: vīrēs mē dēficiunt, my strength is failing. Traupman uses it for running low: argentum mihi … paululum dēficit (p. 91).

evidence: Cic. Fam. 1.9.17 (Lewis & Short): ut neque amīcīs neque etiam aliēniōribus operā, cōnsiliō, labōre dēsim
Traupman 102: alicuī deesse, to let someone down
terms.comment: Words fail me: mihi verba dēsunt (Traupman 111, 408).

phrases.english: It was not nature that failed, but care.

phrases.latin: Numquam ubi diū fuit ignis, dēfēcit vapor.
phrases.english: Where there has long been a fire, the warmth never fails.

phrases.latin: quod petis, hīc est, est Ulubrīs, animus sī tē nōn dēficit aequus
phrases.english: What you are looking for is here, it is at Ulubrae, if a level mind does not fail you.

sources: Lewis & Short: deficio · Lewis & Short: desum
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 91, 102, 111, 342, 373, 408, checked against the searchable text of the book (9 November 2026).
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-quintilianus, loci-publilius, loci-horatius), checked against the editions named there.
Publilius is cited as the loci collection numbers him, by position under each initial letter in the Latin Library text; from N onwards that numbering differs from Meyer’s.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
